articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA)
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. This action targets entities involved in activities that undermine American intellectual property rights.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued associated General Licenses to provide guidance and authorization for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited. The specifics of these licenses aim to mitigate unintended consequences while maintaining the integrity of the sanctions program.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and Issues New FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 16, 2026. This update aims to clarify the scope of authorized activities and provide further guidance to the public regarding U.S. sanctions on Venezuela.

The amendment and FAQ are part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to fine-tune sanctions programs, ensuring they remain effective in achieving policy goals while minimizing undue burdens on legitimate humanitarian and commercial activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran and Cuba Designations, Issues General Licenses and FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations related to Iran and a specific designation concerning Cuba on October 15, 2026. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter illicit financial activities and support for destabilizing actors in both regions.

In addition to the designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) to provide clarity on the scope of the new restrictions and to authorize certain transactions. The Iran-related sanctions targeted two offshore banks affiliated with Bank Mellat and Bank Shahr, an Iraqi bank, and a network involved in Iranian oil sales, under 'Operation Economic Outcast'. The Cuba designation targeted Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA) due to its ties to Iran.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026. This action signifies a recalibration of sanctions policy, potentially in response to evolving circumstances or compliance efforts by the delisted entity.
Designation removals are a standard part of OFAC's sanctions programs, reflecting a dynamic approach to foreign policy objectives and the impact of sanctions on designated individuals and entities.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities on October 13, 2026. These actions aim to disrupt financial networks supporting illicit drug trafficking and terrorist organizations globally.

These designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating transnational criminal enterprises and safeguarding the international financial system from abuse by those who seek to fund terrorism and drug-related activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics; Designates International Criminal Court Officials
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026, for apparent violations of sanctions programs. Concurrently, OFAC also announced designations related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued associated General Licenses.

In a separate action, a Burma-related designation was removed, indicating a review and adjustment of sanctions as circumstances evolve. These actions highlight OFAC's multi-faceted approach to enforcing sanctions and addressing various foreign policy concerns.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This license provides authorization for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under existing sanctions against Russia.

The issuance of General Licenses is a common practice by OFAC to ensure that sanctions are implemented effectively while allowing for legitimate activities and minimizing unintended humanitarian or economic consequences.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations and Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and issued an Iran-related General License on October 8, 2026. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter the Iranian regime's illicit activities and its support for destabilizing regional actors.

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License, indicating adjustments to existing sanctions against Russia. These changes reflect the dynamic nature of sanctions policy, adapting to evolving geopolitical landscapes and specific policy objectives.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Designation Removals and Updates, Publishes Iran-Related Alert
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced several designation removals and updates on October 5, 2026. These actions reflect ongoing reviews of sanctions lists and adjustments based on new information or changes in circumstances.

Concurrently, OFAC published an Iran-related Alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). The alert warns foreign financial institutions about the risks of doing business with Iran's financial sector under 'Operation Economic Outcast,' emphasizing potential sanctions for those transacting with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions.

articles.headline: EU Adopts Largest Sanctions Package Against Russia's Military-Industrial Complex
body: The European Union adopted its largest-ever package of restrictive measures against Russia on October 12, 2026, targeting 1,569 individuals and entities within Russia's military and industrial complex. This action brings the total number of listings under the Russia sanctions regime to nearly 4,600.

The new sanctions specifically target mid-level suppliers that form the core of the Russian military industry, including companies supplying key components for advanced weapons systems such as missiles, UAVs, and aircraft. The listed entities are subject to an asset freeze, and individuals face a travel ban to the EU.

This package is a direct response to Russia's continued aggression against Ukraine, including missile and drone strikes against civilian targets and critical infrastructure. The EU aims to restrict Russia's access to key military products and components, thereby impeding its military industrial production.
articles.source: Council of the EU / Hill Dickinson / Ministry for Foreign Affairs / Morgan Lewis / The National Law Review

articles.headline: EU Sanctions Three Individuals and Four Entities Over DPRK Nuclear and Missile Programs, Russia Ties
body: The Council of the European Union adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities on October 12, 2026, under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK). These designations target those responsible for supporting, promoting, or facilitating activities contributing to the DPRK's nuclear weapons, ballistic missile, or other weapons of mass destruction programs, as well as for violating and evading United Nations sanctions.

The new listings specifically address activities linked to the growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, including the deployment of DPRK workers in Russia, commercial and industrial cooperation, and an 'arms-for-oil' trade, all in violation of UN Security Council prohibitions.

The sanctioned entities include Paekyangsan Shipping Co Ltd, involved in shipments of refined petroleum products from Russia to North Korea, and Golden Autumn Agroholding, a subsidiary of the Russian holding company Black Horse, whose founder was also sanctioned for promoting Russia-North Korea industrial projects.
articles.source: Council of the EU / Consilium.europa.eu / The Brussels Times / Africanews

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026, resulting in a civil penalty of $11,662,930. This penalty addresses apparent violations of numerous U.S. sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

This OFAC penalty is part of a broader enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also saw significant fines from FinCEN and the OCC for anti-money laundering failures. The combined penalties against Bank of America exceeded $1.21 billion.

Bank of America admitted to 475 apparent sanctions violations, highlighting systemic issues in its compliance program. The Treasury Department emphasized that even the largest financial institutions are not exempt from sanctions and AML laws.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / FinCEN / U.S. Department of the Treasury / Zyphe / Banking Dive

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has reached a settlement agreement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 9, 2026, agreeing to pay a civil penalty of $175,015. The settlement addresses apparent violations of OFAC-administered sanctions programs.

This enforcement action underscores OFAC's continued vigilance in ensuring compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations across various industries, including logistics and shipping. Companies are reminded of the importance of robust compliance programs to prevent sanctions breaches.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1,427,230 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations

The penalty serves as a reminder that individuals involved in transactions that violate U.S. sanctions can face significant financial repercussions. OFAC continues to emphasize the importance of due diligence and adherence to sanctions regulations by all U.S. persons.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty on Bank of America for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026, for widespread breakdowns in its Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program. This represents the largest civil money penalty in OCC history.

The OCC found that Bank of America's BSA/AML compliance program was deficient and ineffective, with its transaction monitoring system failing to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions. This led to a large number of late Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars, many of which had indicia of money laundering.

This action follows a December 2024 cease-and-desist order that required the bank to address its BSA/AML deficiencies. Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan V. Gould stated that the bank's poor response to these deficiencies was unacceptable, warranting the significant penalty.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / U.S. Department of the Treasury / Zyphe / Banking Dive

articles.headline: FinCEN Assesses $1.2 Billion Penalty Against Bank of America for BSA Violations
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) announced a $1.2 billion civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026, for willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA). This penalty is the third-largest in Treasury history and addresses the bank's failures to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese money laundering networks and illicit finance along the southwest border.

FinCEN found that Bank of America failed to implement and maintain an adequate AML program, conduct due diligence for correspondent accounts for foreign financial institutions, and file Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) in a timely manner. The bank admitted to failing to timely report over $5 billion of suspicious activity between 2018 and 2025.

As part of the resolution, FinCEN credited the $750 million civil money penalty assessed concurrently by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) for the bank's deficient BSA/AML compliance program.
articles.source: FinCEN / U.S. Department of the Treasury / Arc-Serv, LLC. / Zyphe / Banking Dive

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
